title: Construction and Setup of a Bench-scale Algal Photosynthetic Bioreactor with Temperature, Light, and pH Monitoring for Kinetic Growth Tests
protocol: Construct the Bench-scale PBR Body and Lid.
Determine the PBR volume required for the research needs.
Determine the experimental objectives for this PBR.
Decide which algal measurement assays are necessary to characterize the growth of the algal species of interest.
Calculate the volume required per assay, v.
Determine the number of technical replicates, n.
Set the sampling frequency, f.
Define the duration of experiments, t.
Calculate the total culture volume required for sampling throughout one experiment using Equation 6.
Estimate a target PBR volume using Vs from step 1.1.3 and a maximum volume removal fraction, F, using Equation 7.
Select sensors and accessories for the PBR experiments.
Choose pH, light, and temperature probes for continuous monitoring.
Select an impeller design and motor to satisfy mixing requirements.
Use a low-shear, axial impeller for Dunaliella algae.
Employ a 12 V mini-gear motor for low mixing speeds.
Assemble the PBR body and lid.
Determine the dimensions of the reactor based on volume calculations.
Cut five pieces of optically clear cast acrylic sheets using a table saw.
Smooth the joint edges with 200 to 400 grit sandpaper, avoiding rounding.
Secure the edges of the acrylic pieces together with tape and/or clamps.
Apply acrylic cement along the joints in a well-ventilated area.
Allow the pieces to sit for 24 hours.
Apply viscous acrylic cement to the joints to ensure watertightness.
Leave the cement to dry for 24-48 hours, according to the instructions.
Fill the reactor with water to check for visible leaks.
Place the reactor on paper towels and recheck for signs of leakage after 24-36 hours.
Set up and configure sensors with the data acquisition and control unit.
Set up and configure the light sensor with the data acquisition and control unit using a low-pass filter.
Cut a 2 inch piece of green connector wire.
Strip 0.25 in of insulation off one end of the green connector wire.
Strip approximately 0.5 in of insulation off the other end of the green connector wire.
Identify the analog signal output wire on the light sensor.
Ensure at least 0.25-0.50 inches of metal wire are exposed past the wire insulation.
Wrap one leg of the 1,000 Ω resistor around the ~0.5 inch stripped end of the connector wire.
Wrap the other leg of the resistor around the exposed section of the light sensor analog signal wire.
Solder the resistor legs to the wire using a soldering iron and lead-free solder.
Allow the solder to cool for 2-5 min.
Slip a ~1.5 inch piece of heat-shrink tubing over one end of the connector wire.
Slide the heat-shrink tubing until it covers the soldered wire and resistor.
Heat-shrink the tubing using a heat gun.
Attach the ground wire of the light sensor to a free GND terminal on the data acquisition and control unit using a screwdriver.
Secure the free end of the signal connector wire to a free analog input (AIN) terminal using a screwdriver.
Secure the positive lead of the 1,000 µF capacitor to the same AIN terminal as in step 2.1.8.
Secure the negative lead of the 1,000 µF capacitor to the same GND terminal as in step 2.1.7.
Ensure that both the capacitor leg and the wire are firmly connected to the terminal.
Identify the power input wire for the light sensor.
Secure this wire to a voltage supply (VS) terminal on the data acquisition and control unit.
Set up and configure the pH electrode with the data acquisition unit using a unity-gain amplifier.
Connect the unity-gain amplifier to the pH probe using the transmitter wire.
Connect the co-axial adapter, with positive and negative port terminals, to the other end of the unity-gain amplifier.
Cut two 6-inch pieces of green connector wire using wire strippers.
Strip ~0.25 inch of insulation off both ends of each green connector wire.
Cut one ~12-inch piece of black connector wire using wire strippers.
Strip ~0.25 inch and ~0.5 inch of insulation off both ends of the black connector wire.
Wrap one leg of the 1,000 Ω resistor around the ~0.5 inch stripped section of one green connector wire.
Wrap the other resistor leg around the ~0.5 inch stripped section of the other green connector wire.
Use a soldering iron and lead-free solder to solder the resistor legs to the wire.
Allow the solder to cool for 2-5 minutes.
Slip a ~1.5 inch piece of heat-shrink tubing over one end of the connector wire and slide it until it covers the soldered wire and resistor.
Heat-shrink using a heat gun.
Secure one end of the black connector wire to the negative (black) terminal post on the co-axial adapter.
Insert the other end of this wire into a GND terminal of the data acquisition and control unit and secure using a screwdriver.
Secure one end of the green connector wire (with the resistor in series) to the positive (red) terminal post on the co-axial adapter.
Insert the other end of this connector wire into a free AIN terminal on the data acquisition and control unit.
Identify the positive lead of the 1,000 µF capacitor and secure it to the same AIN terminal as in step 2.2.9.
Secure the negative lead of the 1,000 µF capacitor to the same GND terminal as in step 2.2.8.
Connect the temperature sensor to the data acquisition and control unit by connecting the signal, ground, and power wires of the probe to free AIN, GND, and VS terminals.
Connect the data acquisition and control unit to a computer near the experimental setup using a USB cable.
Download all required drivers for the data acquisition and control unit.
Open the data acquisition and control software on the computer.
Set up 'Conversions' for each sensor in the software.
Navigate to "Conversions" in the software workspace, on the right side of the main homepage.
Add a conversion name such as "volts_to_celsius".
Type in the conversion equation: (55.56 x value) + 255.37 - 273.15.
Navigate to the "Channel" page within the software.
Add a sensor channel name.
Select the appropriate device to collect data for the corresponding channel.
Input the device number for the data acquisition and control unit or other data-acquiring device.
Select analog-to-digital, “A to D,” for the input-output type (“I/O Type”).
Input the channel number corresponding to the AIN terminal number on the data acquisition and control unit.
Input the desired sampling timing (s); this value indicates how often the sensor signal will be read.
Input 1.0 to acquire a reading every 1 s.
Check the “Avg” box to average data over 1-min intervals prior to logging and specify 60 for the averaging length.
Select the appropriate conversion from the dropdown menu if applicable; otherwise, all channel data will be displayed/recorded as voltage.
Set up the "Logging Set" to log experimental data.
Navigate to the “Logging Panel” within the software workspace and add a new logging set.
Name the logging set accordingly.
Select the output file type and location; choose ASCII file type for comma-separated value file if the extension ‘.csv’ is specified in the output file name.
Add all desired channels to log to this set.
Start logging by right-clicking on the logging sequence in the workspace and selecting the appropriate option.
Stop logging as desired by right-clicking on the logging sequence in the workspace and selecting the appropriate option.
Calibrate the pH probe before every experiment.
Calibrate at the intended temperature of the experiment.
Update pH channel conversions accordingly.
Repeat calibration process after running experimental setup.
Compare readings to determine drift extent.
Properly store pH electrode in storage solution before and after experimentation.
Connect pH and temperature sensors as described in step 2.
Insert pH electrode into pH calibration buffer 7.
Ensure temperature reading matches desired experimental temperature.
Allow pH electrode voltage output to stabilize.
Use graphical display to confirm stabilization.
Log both temperature and pH electrical data for 30-60 seconds.
Do not apply conversions or averaging during logging process.
Repeat the calibration for buffers 4 and 10.
Confirm that the sensor response is between -57 and -59 mV/pH.
Generate a conversion equation by plotting pH buffer value versus voltage and fitting a line.
Update the conversion equation as described in step 3.3.
Apply this conversion to the pH channel.
Update channel settings to include averaging for logging.
Set up the PBR inside a temperature-controlled incubator with accessories and sensors.
Connect the pH and temperature wires to the data acquisition and control unit, as described in steps 2.2-2.3.
Calibrate and update the conversion equation for the pH channel, as described in steps 3.3 and 4.
Thread the light sensor wire through the lid port of the PBR.
Mount the sensor head onto the lid extension mount using a screw.
Use a rubber stopper or grommet to keep the lid port closed to the atmosphere.
Attach and secure the mixer impeller shaft over the DC mini-gear motor shaft inside the PBR lid.
Secure the shaft with a set screw and an Allen wrench.
Add algae-specific growth medium to the PBR.
Place the lid onto the PBR and secure it with screws.
Insert the temperature probe into its designated port in the PBR.
Secure the temperature probe into the port using a rubber stopper.
Secure the pH probe into the reactor lid port using a PG-13.5 threaded mount.
Connect the light sensor wires to the data acquisition unit as described.
Power the mixer impeller to the desired speed.
Set up the variable DC power supply adjacent to the PBR setup.
Turn on the power supply and adjust the voltage knob until it reads 0 volts.
Disconnect all wires before connecting the impeller motor power lines to the positive and negative output terminals of the variable power supply.
Turn on the power supply and slowly increase the voltage by turning the voltage knob until the desired mixing speed is reached.
Calculate the mixing speed by measuring the rotations per min.
Set up the grow lamp to illuminate the PBR.
Select a high-powered, LED grow lamp that emits in the blue and red spectrum.
Ensure the size and shape of the light fixture evenly illuminates the incident surface of the PBR.
Verify that the incubator can handle an internal heat source.
Center the grow lamp along the front face of the PBR.
Make sure that the light path is directly oriented towards the light sensor mounted on the back of the reactor.
Turn on the light.
Adjust the light intensity as needed.
Check the sensor variable display for light readings.
Monitor and log the sensor data for 6 - 24 hours.
Ensure that the light, temperature, and pH readings within the PBR are stable and within the desired range.
Remove electrical noise from the sensor readings.
Remove the rubber stopper on the sampling port.
Add algae inoculum via transfer pipette.
Remove samples to monitor conditions.
Monitor conditions to ensure they stay within the desired range for the experiment.
Remove cultures for analysis as needed using a pipette.
Check the data display in the software for water temperature.
Manually adjust the incubator air temperature set point to keep the water temperature constant.
Monitor and adjust the pH within the PBR as needed.
Control the pH with a 12 V solenoid valve connected to a compressed CO2 tank.
Open the valve as required using the control functionality of the data acquisition and control unit and software.
